en: Sutta Nipāta 2.14 Dhammikasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the lay follower Dhammika, together with five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the lay follower Dhammika...
The lay follower addressed the Blessed One with verses:
“I ask you, Gotama of vast wisdom:
How acting is a disciple truly good?”
Whether one goes from home to homelessness,
or remains at home as a lay follower—
you indeed [are the refuge] for the world together with its devas.
You understand the destination and the final goal;
there is no one equal to you who perceives the subtle meaning.
For they call you, O Buddha, the most excellent.
Having realized for yourself the entire Dhamma through knowledge,
you have proclaimed it out of compassion for beings;
you are one whose eyes are opened, possessing universal vision.
You shine, stainless one, throughout the entire world.
Having heard, "The Victor named Erāvaṇa, the king of nāgas, has come into your presence," [he approached].
Having consulted with her, he too understood;
hearing "So be it," he was filled with great joy.
King Vessavaṇa Kuvera also [acted] toward him.
He approaches the Dhamma, inquiring about it;
and when questioned by him, you, O Wise One, explain it to him,
and he too, having heard it, becomes one who has attained confidence.
Whatever sectarian teachers there may be who are fond of debate,
whether they be Ājīvakas or Nigaṇṭhas—
all of them fail to surpass you in wisdom.
Like one standing still watching another who moves with swift pace—
whatever these brahmins may be, habituated to debate,
there are some brahmins here who are even advanced in years.
All those who hold to their own views, as well as other disputants who imagine themselves right, find their purpose centered in you;
for this Dhamma is subtle and blissful.
O Best of Buddhas, since this Blessed One has been well-served by you,
let all of us who are desirous of hearing it likewise hear it; being asked, please speak to us.
All these monks are seated here,
and likewise the lay followers to hear;
let them listen to the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One.
“Just as the gods [praise] the well-spoken words of Vāsava.
“Listen to me, O bhikkhus; I shall proclaim it to you:
the Dhamma of ascetic purification—practice that, all of you!”
One who sees the goal and possesses wisdom should practice the modes of conduct appropriate for one gone forth.
A bhikkhu should certainly not wander about at the wrong time.
One should wander for alms in the village at the proper time;
for attachments cling to one who wanders at the wrong time.
Therefore, the Buddhas do not wander at the wrong time.
Forms, sounds, tastes, and smells,
and touches that intoxicate beings—
one should subdue desire for these phenomena.
He should enter for his morning meal at the proper time.
Having received almsfood at the right occasion,
the bhikkhu should return alone and sit in seclusion.
Thinking inwardly, his mind does not go outward;
having restrained his self-existence, he should not let it issue forth.
Even if he should converse with a disciple, [he should do so with mindfulness].
Or by some other monk; he should proclaim that sublime Dhamma,
neither through slander nor through speaking ill of others.
For some oppose debate;
we do not praise those of limited wisdom,
who fall into attachments here and there.
For they direct your mind toward things far away:
alms-food, the monastery, lodgings,
and even the removal of dust from your outer robe with a fan.
Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Sugata,
a disciple of noble wisdom should practice with discernment.
Therefore, regarding alms-food, bedding, and seats—
And even when carrying the dust of his outer robe,
the bhikkhu remains unsmeared by these things,
just as a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
But I shall tell you the duty of the householder,
so that by practicing it, a disciple becomes excellent;
for this cannot be attained by one who possesses attachments.
To touch the entirety of the bhikkhu’s dhamma:
one should not kill a living being,
nor cause another to kill, nor approve of others who are killing.
Having laid aside the rod toward all beings—
those that are stationary and those that move which exist in the world—
one should therefore avoid taking what is not given.
A disciple awakening to anything anywhere should neither take what is being taken away nor approve of those who take it;
he should avoid taking everything that is not given.
A wise person should avoid unchastity as they would a pit of glowing embers;
yet, if one is unable to practice the holy life, [one should still refrain from it].
One should not transgress against another’s wife.
Whether in an assembly or in a gathering,
one should not speak falsely even to a single person.
One should not speak what is false, nor should one approve of those who speak it;
one should avoid all that is untrue.
One should not practice the drinking of intoxicants.
The householder who delights in this Dhamma,
knowing it to lead to endless madness, would neither drink himself nor allow others who are drinking.
For fools, intoxicated, commit evil deeds,
and they cause other people who are heedless to do so as well;
one should avoid this source of demerit.
Intoxicating, deluding, and dear to the foolish.
One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given,
nor speak falsehood, nor be a drinker of intoxicants.
One should abstain from unchastity and sexual intercourse;
one should not eat at night or at improper times.
One should not wear garlands nor use perfumes.
One may lie on a bed or on the ground spread with grass;
for this indeed is called the Eightfold Uposatha,
proclaimed by the Buddha who has reached the end of suffering.
And then, with a mind full of serene faith,
he observed the Uposatha days of the fortnight— the fourteenth, the fifteenth,
and the eighth— as well as the fortnight of miracles.
Endowed with eight factors, perfectly complete in form.
Then, having observed the Uposatha in the morning,
he [honored] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with food and drink.
With a clear mind and feeling gratitude,
a wise person should share [the merit] as is fitting;
they should support their mother and father in accordance with the Dhamma.
One should engage in righteous trade;
practicing this as a householder with diligence,
one goes to the gods named Sayampabha.
The Dhammika Sutta, the fourteenth.
The Second Chapter: The Minor Section (Cūḷavagga).
Its summary verse:
The fragrance of jewels and moral shame,
the auspiciousness of Sūciloma,
and the practice of the Dhamma by the brahmin—
The Boat, the Fist, the Origin;
Rāhula, and again Kappa,
and likewise Paribbājaniya;
The wise say that the Dhammika and the Cūḷavagga consist of fourteen [chapters].
